editorial.summary: Jim Rugg and Ed Piskor inspect physical copies of SPX 2000, NON and the Xeric edition of Slow Jams, tracing David Choe's short comics path while reading his collage, photocopy, lettering and autobiographical techniques. The page map preserves the bicycle-revenge story, explicit masturbation spread, infatuation and violent fantasy, suicide turn, prison short, sticker-art encouragement and dated scarcity pitch while separating printed-object evidence, criticism, plot, autobiography, literal biography, rights and safety.

quality.assessment: Complete chronological human read and object-centered correction/context pass. Dense alternative-comics names, titles, grant terms and story-character damage are repaired where defensible. Unclear names and masked words remain unresolved; automatic captions contain no publisher speaker prefixes.

editorial.speaker_policy: The public hosts are Jim Rugg and Ed Piskor, but participant presence does not identify individual lines. Publish no named turns until held-out acoustic/video validation passes.

connections.relationship: SPX 2000 situates Choe among a dense alternative-comics cohort rather than treating him as an isolated celebrity artist.
Pasted text and hand lettering show the page as assembled object, not only drawing.
NON #3 and #4 connect a self-made mini-comic to a curated anthology audience.
NON #5's silkscreened package makes binding and production part of the archive evidence.
The bicycle story uses Choe's persona while the archive resists treating every plot event as literal biography.
The hosts use McCloud's transition framework to explain why Choe's image links feel less cinematic and more associative.
Waiting and a threatening note build anticipation that ends in emotional failure rather than triumph.
Destroying the recovered bicycle preserves the injury without resolving the protagonist's loss.
The hosts argue visual experiment works because autobiographical narration keeps emotional orientation.
The perfect-bound book is linked backward to a mini-comic and sideways to NON serialization.
A best-of issue functions as a pre-algorithm recommendation system for alternative comics.
Kochalka, McCloud and Young quotations show multiple critical vocabularies attaching to the debut.
Street sensibility and believable characters prompt a comparison with Jaime Hernandez rather than a claim of direct influence.
An abstinence text becomes visual material inside an explicitly sexual autobiographical book.
A released prisoner choosing a return is presented as a short fictional tragedy, not a universal claim about reentry.
The masturbation spread makes duration calculable through repeated actions and linked images.
Formal innovation does not by itself settle whether an explicit page belongs in a classroom.
A detailed face within visual chaos demonstrates how Choe controls focal hierarchy.
The annual meeting promise transforms a letter into a multi-year fantasy structure.
A wished-for reunion turns into organized humiliation and violence.
The hospital escape and suicidal turn are plot events requiring context, not isolated biographical claims.
The story moves from violent fantasy and self-destruction to a private reaffirmation rather than a clean rescue moral.
Grant evidence connects material production to a broader cohort of self-published cartoonists.
The hosts value Choe's looseness because it challenges their own fear of carrying sketchbook energy onto final pages.
